item.title: World Bank-backed initiative attracts $300m in private investment
item.description:
Bangladesh's economic zones have attracted nearly US$300 million in private investment with support from the World Bank, creating around 42,000 new jobs.
The investment has helped create employment opportunities and expand business development prospects in the country's economic zones, contributing to efforts to build a stronger and more resilient economy, according to a post by the World Bank Bangladesh on its official Facebook page.
The World Bank highlighted the achievements as part of its efforts to mobilize private capital and promote investment-led economic growth in Bangladesh.
The initiative underscores the potential of economic zones to attract domestic and foreign investors, generate employment and strengthen the country's industrial base.
The World Bank's post also emphasized the role of private capital mobilization in creating opportunities for businesses and supporting Bangladesh's long-term economic development.

item.title: Marcel Digital Campaign Season 25 kicks off
item.description:
Marcel has launched its nationwide ‘Digital Campaign Season 25.’ Under this season, customers are offered attractive rewards on purchasing Marcel refrigerator, television, air conditioner or ceiling fan.
The rewards include gifts of free products, foreign trip, cashback and guaranteed gifts. The customers will enjoy these rewards until December 31, 2026.
Recently, Marcel Digital Campaign Season-25 was inaugurated at Marcel’s corporate office in the campital.
Company’s chairman SM Shamsul Alam, vice chairman SM Ashraful Alam, and managing director SM Mahbubul Alam joined the event virtually and addressed the participants.
Marcel officials announced that customers will complete the digital registration using his/her name, mobile number and mobile phone numbers after they had purchased Marcel refrigerators, televisions, air conditioners or ceiling fans during the campaign.
After the registration, a fully computerized system will then determine their gifts. Customers will receive an SMS notification with the details, and the respective showroom will hand over their gifts.
The campaign’s houseful gifts of free products’ includes refrigerators, air conditioners, smart televisions, washing machines, microwave ovens, gas stoves, infrared cookers, rice cookers, blenders, ceiling fans, rechargeable fans, water heaters, irons, electric kettles and other appliances.
Chairman SM Shamsul Alam said that Marcel customers were benefiting significantly from the digital campaign, which had received an enthusiastic response nationwide. Considering the customers’ sound response to the digital campaign, Season 25 has been launched across the country.
Vice chairman SM Ashraful Alam said that the company always emphasizes on providing highest benefits and services to strengthen customer satisfaction and trust. As part of this effort, the ‘Digital Campaign Season 25’ was launched offering a wide range of essential home appliances.
He urged Marcel distributors, sales representatives and all other related officials to work together to encourage customer spontaneous participation in Season-25.
Managing director SM Mahbubul Alam said, Marcel products are durable, energy-efficient and affordable. The company also works to provide customers with prompt, best after-sales service. He advised those involved to strengthen promotional activities nationwide to inform customers about these product features and the campaign’s gifts and benefits.
The ceremony was hosted by Marcel brand ambassador and film actor Amin Khan.
Additional managing director Eva Rizwana Nilu, Marcel head of business Md Ruhin Sabbir, chief marketing officer Joheb Ahmed, and other senior officials attended the event.
In addition, Marcel distributors and sales representatives from across the country also joined the event through digital platform.
Marcel is developing a digital customer database to make after-sales service faster and more automated. Following a purchase, customer names, mobile numbers, product barcodes and other necessary information are stored on the company’s own server through digital registration.
This enables customers to access service easily at any Marcel service centre in the country, even if they lose their warranty cards.
Marcel regularly organizes digital campaigns to encourage customers to participate in this registration process.

item.title: 12kg gold paste seized at Dhaka airport
item.description:
Customs officials seized 12 kg of gold paste, worth an estimated Tk24 crore, from two passengers arriving from Dubai at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on Wednesday.
The gold paste, initially confirmed to be 24-carat gold through preliminary testing, was concealed in the jeans and underwear of the two passengers, identified as Chen Liyun and Mo Xiaoyu.
According to Dhaka Customs House, its preventive team launched surveillance at different points of the airport following a tip-off that gold might be smuggled into the country on Emirates flight EK586 from Dubai.
The team intercepted the two passengers after they completed immigration formalities and arrived at baggage carousel-2.
During searches, customs officials found soft, yellow-coloured gold paste concealed inside their clothing and stitched into fabric.
The seized gold paste weighed 12 kg in its wet state, while its estimated market value stands at Tk24 crore, the customs authorities said.

item.title: Four crude bombs recovered from garage in South Keraniganj
item.description:
A team of Special Response Battalion (SRB)-10 recovered four unexploded crude bombs from a garage in the Shuvaddya area of South Keraniganj in Dhaka district on Wednesday afternoon.
The bombs were found abandoned during a special drive conducted by an operational team of SRB-10’s Sadar Company at around 5:10pm.
Tapan Sarkar, senior assistant superintendent of police (Media) of SRB-10, said the operation was launched based on secret information about the buying and selling of illegal drugs and other items in the area.
All four crude bombs were recovered unexploded, he said.
SRB-10 said it follows a zero-tolerance policy towards such crimes and remains committed to maintaining law and order and bringing offenders to justice.
The battalion also said it would continue its efforts to prevent threats to public safety and the state while performing its duties professionally.

item.title: JU admission tests to begin on January 10
item.description:
Jahangirnagar University (JU) will hold admission tests for first-year undergraduate programs for the 2026-27 academic session from January 10 to 21, 2027, with examinations scheduled on all days except Fridays and Saturdays.
Syed Mohammad Ali Reza, deputy registrar of the university’s Education Branch, confirmed the schedule to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday.
“Our first meeting on admission-related matters was held today (Wednesday), and several decisions were made regarding the admission tests,” he said.
The examinations will be held on the university campus, as plans to conduct tests in divisional cities will not be implemented this year, Reza said.
No final decision has been made on admission test fees, although the issue was discussed at the meeting. The university has also yet to complete its review of the admission test results, with final decisions on these matters likely to be made at the next meeting, he added.
The unit structure will remain unchanged from last year. However, according to the meeting’s decisions, the Law Department will come under the Faculty of Social Sciences for this year’s admission tests.

item.title: Shadman stranded on 99 as Bangladesh dominate opening day
item.description:
Opener Shadman Islam was left stranded on 99 as bad light brought a premature end to the opening day of the first Test against West Indies, with Bangladesh firmly in control at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium today.
Shadman struck 10 fours in a patient knock that helped Bangladesh recover from an early setback and finish the day on front foot. The hosts had reached 213-3 when play was called off, with Shadman unbeaten on 99 and Liton Das on 10.
Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto won the toss and elected to bat, a decision that eventually paid off as Shadman displayed a remarkable composure against a disciplined West Indies bowling attack.
New ball bowlers Jayden Seales and Shamar Joseph immediately put the Bangladesh openers under pressure with probing lines and lengths. Their persistence paid off when Tanzid Hasan Tamim, on 7, edged a delivery outside off stump to the second slip.
Shadman, however, resisted the temptation to drive outside off and patiently rebuilt the innings alongside Mominul Haque. The pair frustrated the West Indies pacers with a 59-run partnership.
Left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican broke the stand when Mominul sliced a delivery to mid-off, departing for 28 off 51 balls, including two fours.Warrican then removed Shanto for 19 after a successful leg-before-wicket review, with the Bangladesh captain missing a paddle sweep.
Shadman reached his 10th Test half-century, and fourth against West Indies, off 95 balls, guiding a delivery behind square on the leg side for a single.He subsequently found an able partner in Towhid Hridoy, who was playing his first Test since making his debut in Harare in July this year.
Hridoy began positively, striking an easy boundary off Shamar Joseph before producing an impressive pull against the same bowler.
The pair added 88 runs to bolster Bangladesh's position before Hridoy was forced to leave the field after suffering cramps in the humid conditions. He was batting on 42.
Shadman continued to accumulate runs steadily, punishing loose deliveries while maintaining his discipline against the probing attack.
Bad light first interrupted play for around 30 minutes when Shadman was on 96. After the resumption, the left-hander moved closer to his third Test century, only to be denied the opportunity to reach the milestone before the day's play was abandoned.
Liton, returning to the side after recovering from a hip joint injury, was unbeaten on 10 when the umpires called off play.
Warrican was the most successful bowler for West Indies, ending the day with 2-33.
Brief Scores: Day 1
Bangladesh 213 for 3 (Shadman 99*, Hridoy 42, Warrican 2-33) vs West Indies

item.title: Death toll from drone strike in Sudan’s Darfur rises to 102
item.description:
The death toll from an army drone strike on a market in the Sudanese city of Nyala has risen to 102, a rights group said Wednesday, in the latest deadly attack on the paramilitary stronghold in western Darfur.
Sudan’s military, at war with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has established an administration rivalling the army-backed, internationally recognized government in Khartoum.
Witnesses and a medical source initially told AFP the strike killed 21 people and injured 40 others.
The Emergency Lawyers, which has been documenting abuses throughout Sudan’s war, later said the toll stood at 102, with another 113 people wounded, including women and children.
According to the group, a drone struck Tanqonj Market, a busy civilian marketplace where residents gather to buy daily necessities and earn a living.
Residents described devastating losses.
“I lost my 19-year-old son in Monday’s market strike. We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site,” Hamdan Suleiman, a resident of Nyala’s Doumaya neighborhood, told AFP via a text message.
Another resident, Zahra Hamidan, who sells food in the market, said several workers were killed “next to my food stall.”
Sudan’s war, now in its fourth year, is increasingly being fought through drone attacks, with both sides carrying out long-range strikes that have killed scores of civilians.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone attacks killed more than 300 people and wounded hundreds more, according to the UN.

item.title: Houthis say Saudi Arabia conducted deadly strikes as they target Aden
item.description:
Yemen’s Houthis said Saudi strikes on a petrol station and a market killed more than a dozen people on Wednesday, while the Iran-backed group targeted the perimeter of the airport in government stronghold Aden.
The Houthis last month launched a lightning offensive in Yemen, reigniting a long frozen civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government there.
They have also launched sustained attacks on Saudi Arabia itself, the world’s biggest crude exporter, rattling global markets already volatile from the wider Middle East war.
On Wednesday, Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead “and 15 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll,” in attacks it blamed on Saudi Arabia in the northwestern Jawf province, where it reported strikes on a market and a petrol station.
In Aden, a Houthi missile fell inside the perimeter of the airport shortly before the group issued a call to evacuate the area, a local police source told AFP. The group targeted the airport again later, another police source said.
“Our armed forces call on those present at Aden airport to immediately evacuate due to the presence of a military cargo plane belonging to the Saudi enemy transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram.
The first strike happened while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane “was not hit and took off shortly afterward,” the first police source said.
The second attack targeted an area “under Saudi forces’ control inside the perimeter of Aden airport,” the second Aden police official said.
Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
The Houthis have targeted Aden several times in recent weeks.
They have also intensified attacks on their Saudi foe, while they battle the government it backs in Aden, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
On Saturday, a police source told AFP that the Houthis targeted a Saudi coalition military position near the Aden airport. It was also targeted the previous week.
Two missiles also landed within the airport perimeter earlier this month, a day after a deadly missile attack struck the presidential palace in Aden.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.

item.title: Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU’s diplomatic blockade?
item.description:
The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar’s military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month.
Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar’s rare-earth resources. The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China.
Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar’s military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts.
The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election, which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president. The military retains control over the political system.
The EU responded to Myanmar’s February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities.
Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months.
At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations.
The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar’s preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country’s garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019.
The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data.
The EU “continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime,” in view of “the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population,” an EU spokesman told DW.
At the same time, the bloc “is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, Asean countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar’s military regime.”
“It also supports Asean efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented,” the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) in 2021.
In the aftermath of the coup, Asean took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar’s military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan.
However, Asean’s position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar’s neighbor Thailand, signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar’s civil war.
Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington’s renewed engagement and suggested that Asean members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar’s future at their summit in Manila next month.
Myanmar’s authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation. In September, Myanmar’s leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments.
On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a “significant shift in approach” after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d’affaires of Myanmar’s military-controlled embassy in London, at an Asean diplomatic gathering days earlier.
According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime’s charge d’affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament’s delegation for Southeast Asia.
Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU’s policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington’s apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta.
The US strategy “appears to be pursuing specific interests” such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said.
However, the most important rare earth mining operations are no longer controlled by the military, but by rebels such as the Kachin Independence Organization in Kachin State. “It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta,” she said.
The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, “so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU’s credibility,” Kironska added.
“At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions.”
The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar’s authorities, the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country’s political future.
Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels’ relations with Myanmar’s democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory.
“The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar’s future,” Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW.
One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through Asean, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace.
Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centered on the military authorities in Naypyidaw.
This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar’s future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said.
For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar’s generals.

item.title: Toll in Nigeria gang attack rises to 62
item.description:
The death toll from an attack by criminal gangs on a Nigerian town last week has jumped to 62 after more bodies were recovered, Nigerian emergency services said Wednesday.
Thousands were also displaced by the violence, according to the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema).
Gunmen from a suspected bandit gang on motorcycles swarmed Binnari, in the northeastern Taraba state shortly after Friday prayers, killing dozens and looting stores.
While northeastern Nigeria is home to a long-running jihadist insurgency, Taraba is also plagued by gangs of criminals, known in the west African country as bandits, who are driven by money rather than ideology or religion.
NEMA said in a statement that the attack “claimed 62 lives and left 52 persons injured,” based on the report it received from the Taraba state emergency services.
A Taraba state police spokesman had told AFP at the weekend that at least 48 people were killed in the violence.
He said 10 bodies were recovered on Friday while 23 more were found in surrounding bushes the following day, along with 15 that drowned in a river while fleeing the attack.
Residents of the town had put the death toll at 50 on Saturday.
The police spokesman did not respond to an AFP inquiry on the new death toll.
“The incident reportedly affected 7,123 persons and displaced 5,187 residents, creating an urgent humanitarian situation in the community,” Nema said in the statement.
The emergency agency said it was working with local authorities to assess the needs of the people displaced by the attack for the provision of “appropriate humanitarian assistance.”
Banditry is a growing problem in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs battling the overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations.
They raid villages and impose levies on farmers and mining operations in areas with little state presence.
Amnesty International, in a post on X, blamed the Nigerian authorities for leaving some rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity.”
“Consistent failure of the authorities to bring the suspected perpetrators to justice is clearly emboldening impunity,” the rights group said on social media.

item.title: Iran warns of ‘devastating’ economic fallout from any new Israeli attack
item.description:
Iran on Wednesday warned of a devastating economic impact from any new Israeli-led attack, as the votes were counted in an Israeli election that could determine the future of the regional war.
Under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has vowed to topple Iran’s government, the two countries have directly fought a war for the first time in their history after decades of enmity.
Tuesday’s pivotal election gave Israelis a chance to offer a verdict on Netanyahu’s right-wing government, amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran following their launch of the war in February.
“Devastating impact on int’l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to recent discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.
Since the war erupted, it has severely disrupted energy shipments from Gulf countries after Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.
Iran has restricted passage and regularly attacks vessels that attempt to cross without its authorization.
In retaliation, the United States has been maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports, seeking to squeeze the country’s economy.
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington had told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible “short, intense military campaign” against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
But the newspaper, citing people briefed on the conversations, said President Donald Trump had not made a final decision.
Netanyahu, vying to form a coalition government after the closely contested polls, has said Israel has an opportunity to eliminate the “existential threat” posed by Iran.
His main electoral rival Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, has warned Israel’s security top brass that they must serve the national interests and not the political needs of Netanyahu.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
On Sunday, Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu and Israeli military chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir had clashed over an order for unspecified military action that defense officials feared could trigger renewed fighting with Iran.
Netanyahu denied the report.
As the votes were counted on Wednesday in the election, no clear winner had emerged between Netanyahu’s bloc and an opposition camp led by Eisenkot.
Tehran has said the outcome of the polls “makes no difference.”
On Sunday, Araghchi said a resumption of war with the US and Israel would also not change Iran’s positions.
“They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past,” he said.
Iran’s military meanwhile has warned it would retaliate more widely against any new attack, with security chief Mohsen Rezaei saying it could strike US-related infrastructure including data centers and other artificial intelligence targets.
Tehran has dismissed Netanyahu’s threats to topple the Iranian government, calling them “empty” and “a sign of desperation.”

item.title: ULAB named finalist in three categories at Global PR Awards 2026
item.description:
The University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB) has been named a finalist in all three categories it entered at the World Public Relations and Communication Awards 2026, recognizing two university initiatives and student Nishat Anjum Anika. Organized by the Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management, the awards recognize excellence in public relations and communication worldwide.
ULAB’s Sustainable Literacy Outreach Effort has been nominated in the Education & Training Campaign category for its community-oriented approach to promoting literacy and sustainable educational development. Its Ode to ULAB Philosophy Campaign has been shortlisted in the Audiovisual category for communicating the university’s institutional philosophy and identity through audiovisual storytelling.
Meanwhile, ULAB student Nishat Anjum Anika has been nominated as a finalist in the Global Student of the Year category, marking a further achievement for the university on the international stage.
The three nominations highlight ULAB’s efforts to strengthen institutional communication, support educational initiatives, promote sustainability, and recognize student achievement.
The winners of the World Public Relations and Communication Awards 2026 are scheduled to be announced at the awards ceremony on 17 November 2026 in Abuja, Nigeria.

item.title: DAB suspends leader over alleged assault on IEDCR director, forms probe panel
item.description:
The Doctors Association of Bangladesh (DAB), a pro-BNP physicians’ organization, has suspended its Assistant Secretary for Legal Affairs, Dr Zahid Hasan Ripok, over the alleged assault on Prof Dr Kazi Ahmed Zaki, director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), inside his office on Wednesday.
It also formed a probe committee to look into the incident, which took place around 11:30am.
Confirming the development, DAB President Prof Dr Harun Al Rashid told UNB that the organization initially identified the main person involved in the incident after reviewing video footage and suspended his membership.
“He has been given 48 hours to explain his position. A probe committee has also been formed,” he said.
Harun said strict organizational action will be taken against the accused if he fails to provide a satisfactory explanation within the stipulated time.
He also made it clear that DAB does not support such disorder or wrongdoing in any way.
The victim and the accused are lifetime members of DAB.
Meanwhile, Leader of the Opposition and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman on Wednesday described the alleged assault on the IEDCR director inside his office as an “act of audacity and a criminal offence”.
“This is undoubtedly an overstepping of limits, an act of audacity and a criminal offence. It must be properly investigated, and those responsible must be brought to justice. Otherwise, the fragile healthcare system will not be able to recover under any circumstances,” he said in a Facebook post.
After the BNP formed the government, the government made Zaki, a public health expert who recently conducted research on the effectiveness of measles vaccines, the IEDCR director.
According to the account of the incident, the director was holding a meeting with several people in his office in the morning when eight to nine individuals suddenly entered the room.
They allegedly pulled him out of his chair and began assaulting him.

item.title: The 18 months that changed Bangladesh
item.description:
In August 2024, the streets of Dhaka smelled of smoke and uncertainty. Autorickshaws fell silent. Shopkeepers pulled down shutters early. The old order had collapsed, and in its place stepped an 84-year-old Nobel laureate who promised to shepherd Bangladesh toward democracy.
Eighteen months later, in February 2026, those same streets erupted in celebration. The BNP won a sweeping victory, and Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister. The transition felt complete, a return to the democratic fold after an unelected interregnum.
But as we mark eight months of the new government, a question lingers: What exactly happened during those 18 months?
The Yunus-led interim government departed, handing over power with farewell speeches about sovereignty and dignity. Yet they left behind a trail of shadowy decisions and unanswered questions.
They governed without an electoral mandate but with immense moral authority, born of a mass uprising. That authority came with an obligation: To be more transparent than any elected government, not less.
We have crossed the bridge back to democracy. But the bridge itself was built with materials that now demand inspection. It is time to light a torch and walk back into that tunnel.
The ledger of lost lives
The most damning indictment of the interim government’s priorities is written in the bodies of dead children.
Bangladesh is now in the grip of the world’s worst measles outbreak. Starting mid-March, over 200,000 have been hospitalized across the country, with the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak being 1,242 as of today. 94% of them were children under five.
In Sylhet, Amin Mia sold the family’s autorickshaw to pay for hospital treatment for his two-year-old son, Arman. The boy died unvaccinated in July. “They came only after I buried my son,” Mia said.
In Chhatak, Humayun Rashid’s nine-month-old daughter Labiba died in June. She was eligible for vaccination in April, when the emergency program lowered the age threshold to six months. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.
The outbreak was preventable. In September 2025, the interim government stopped purchasing vaccines through UNICEF -- a reliable system that had worked for years -- and switched to an open tender system, a move widely suspected to be a precursor to privatizing vaccine procurement.
The tender stalled. Vaccine stock depleted. A planned nationwide campaign was cancelled. By 2025, first-dose coverage had fallen to 90% and second-dose to 86%, both below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity.
The current government reinstated Unicef procurement and launched an emergency campaign in April. But the response has been incomplete.
A Reuters investigation found that the campaign’s target list excluded four million children in the eligible age group. By August, the proportion of confirmed cases who were unvaccinated had actually risen, from 82% to 85%.
The children who died were failed twice: First by the procurement decision, then by the response to its consequences.
The architecture of opacity
When Yunus addressed the nation in those first days, he spoke of transparency. He promised that all advisers would disclose their assets. That promise gathered dust like an abandoned building.
Instead, what emerged was a pattern of decisions that benefited entities intimately connected to the chief adviser himself.
Within two months of Yunus taking office, the National Board of Revenue granted Grameen Bank a five-year income tax exemption until 2029, reversing a 2020 decision. Based on previous records, the bank used to pay around Tk 200 crore annually in taxes, meaning the total revenue loss to the government over five years is estimated to exceed Tk 1,000 crore.
Grameen University, established by Yunus, received approval within three months of applying, while applications from at least 22 other private universities remained pending for years.
Then came the legal reckoning. In September 2026, the High Court ordered Grameen Kalyan, founded by Yunus, to pay Tk 666 crore in outstanding taxes for 2012 through 2017.
The court rejected the organization’s writ petitions, paving the way for the NBR to collect. Jurist Shahdeen Malik said there would be “a certain perception” about the facilities received and that “conflict of interest is another dimension which should have been considered more seriously.”
Transparency International Bangladesh warned that reforms initiated by the interim government had “largely failed” to ensure institutional independence and accountability. TIB concluded that resistance from entrenched interests had derailed much of the interim government’s reform agenda.
The politics of rewriting the past
Perhaps nothing reveals the interim government’s political project more clearly than its enabling of historical erasure.
On February 5, 2025, crowds responding to social media calls for a “bulldozer procession” systematically dismantled the Bangabandhu Memorial Museum at Dhanmondi 32, the historic residence of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The crowd first vandalized and set fire to the museum around 8:30 pm, and by 11:10 pm, an excavator had been brought to the site. Police had deployed additional forces but “did not create any major obstacles to those moving to the museum in processions.”
The interim government issued a statement calling the events “unexpected and unintended.” Transparency International Bangladesh criticized the government’s “alarming nonchalance.”
A case petition was filed against 27 individuals including Yunus and former law adviser Asif Nazrul. The court dismissed it for “lack of grounds.” No arrests have been made. The accused remain free.
The first demolition occurred under the interim government. The precedent was set in February 2025, when an unelected government with a moral mandate to uphold justice stood by while a national museum was demolished by mobs.
The geopolitical gamble
In his farewell address, Yunus declared that Bangladesh had restored its “sovereignty, national interest, and dignity” in foreign policy. But what did this rhetorical sovereignty actually mean in practice?
On February 9, 2026, just three days before the general election, the interim government signed the US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. An analysis of the 32-page agreement found a sharp imbalance in its language: “Bangladesh shall” appears 131 times, while “US shall” appears just six times.
The agreement requires Bangladesh to align with US sanctions regimes, accept US regulatory standards for agricultural products, relax foreign ownership limits in key sectors, and accede to a long list of international intellectual property treaties within specified timelines.
It also embeds binding procurement commitments: 14 Boeing aircraft, approximately $15 billion in American LNG offtake, and 700,000 metric tons of US wheat annually.
The agreement was signed by a government with no electoral mandate, three days before the people it governed were given the chance to choose their own representatives. By what authority did an unelected administration bind the nation to these terms?
The republic’s right to know
An unelected government has no built-in accountability mechanisms. No parliament to answer to. No opposition to monitor its actions. That is precisely why the Yunus government bore a special obligation, a moral obligation, to be more transparent than any elected government could be expected to be.
Yet over 18 months, serious allegations of corruption and abuse of power were raised against several advisers. And they were met with little visible response.
TIB’s Corruption Perceptions Index for 2025 showed Bangladesh’s score rising by only one point to 24, the second-lowest in 14 years. TIB stated that the interim government “failed to take effective and exemplary measures against corruption” and that money laundering had not stopped.
This is not a call for prosecution. It is a call for disclosure. Publish the full text and annexes of the trade agreement. Publish the vaccine procurement timeline. Publish the tax exemption list. Publish the chain of command on Dhanmondi 32.
If the documents show nothing, the interim government is vindicated. If they show something, the public learns what was done in its name. Disclosure does not require a tribunal. It requires a government willing to release paper.
The interim government is gone. But its decisions are not. The trade agreement runs for years. The tax exemptions run to 2029. The measles outbreak is ongoing. The demolition is permanent.
The silence of the current government on these matters is itself part of the story. Why has the new government not repealed the trade agreement, investigated the procurement, or pursued the Dhanmondi 32 case?
The audit demand is not directed only at Yunus. It is directed at whoever currently holds the power to disclose and chooses not to.
We call for a parliamentary commission to review every foreign agreement signed during this period. We call for the full list of tax exemptions received by Yunus and connected institutions to be made public. We call for a full accounting of the vaccine procurement decisions that led to the measles outbreak. The children who died deserve nothing less. And we call for an investigation into the demolition of Dhanmondi 32: Who gave the order, and why no one was held accountable.
These investigations are not intended to defame Yunus or his advisers. They are required in the interest of the nation itself. Examining this interim administration’s powers, responsibilities, and shortcomings can help establish a framework for future caretaker governments. We must assess where mistakes were made or limits exceeded so that similar problems can be avoided in the future.
The citizens of Bangladesh, who braved bullets in July 2024, who demanded democracy, who sacrificed for a better future, deserve nothing less.
They own this republic. They have a right to know what was done in their name during those 18 months when decisions were made in the dark.
The sun has risen on a new government. But shadows remain. Let us chase them out, together.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. His email address is zakir.kibria@gmail.com . Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Who cares for the carers?
item.description:
Most of us have looked after someone who is ill. Even a short illness brings constant questions: Have they had something to drink? Can they wash themselves? Have they slept?
Now imagine asking those questions every day, for years, while caring for a daughter with a disability, a parent with dementia, or a relative with a serious mental health condition.
For unpaid family carers, this is their reality.
They care with love and commitment at enormous personal cost. Their health, livelihoods, education, and social lives can be pushed aside. They hold communities together and sustain health and care systems without pay, recognition, or even a break.
Bangladesh has valued unpaid household and care work at Tk6.7 trillion in 2021, approximately 18.9% of GDP. The calculation includes unpaid domestic work as well as care, but it reveals the scale of a contribution that is too often overlooked.
Bangladesh’s National Healthy Ageing Strategy and Action Plan 2024-2030 acknowledges that family carers can delay or prevent the need for residential care for older people.
Yet recognition in principle is not the same as support in practice. Assistance may go to a person with a disability through the disability allowance or to a household through the Family Card. Too often, nobody looks beneath the surface. Carers are frequently the very people navigating applications and managing payments intended to support someone else.
The evidence from our work in Bangladesh is striking. Through our partnership with the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), research in a project area in Savar found that 67% of households with a carer and a person with a disability were living in extreme poverty, on less than $1 a day.
Separate research highlighted that 95% of family carers in Savar had a health issue or disability of their own. These findings are local, not national estimates, but they expose the pressures hidden behind the word “care.”
Caring has a profoundly disproportionate impact on women. In our three-year program with CDD in Savar, 93% of the 1,008 unpaid family carers supported were women and girls.
For many, caring means giving up paid work, perpetuating financial dependence, and having little time to look after themselves. When we fail to support carers, we deepen inequality for women and girls too.
Consider Kohinoor, a mother in Dhaka caring for her daughter Farea, who has autism. She once struggled alone. Joining a local carers group connected her with people who understood, and she eventually became its president.
With livelihood training, she started poultry rearing. Within two months, her flock had grown from five birds to 12, and she was earning money by selling eggs.
Kohinoor is not an isolated success. Working with CDD, Carers Worldwide has supported 1,008 carers in Savar, established 50 carers groups and trained 425 carers in income-generating activities. Six community caring centres offered children with disabilities care and learning opportunities while giving their carers precious time for work, rest, and social connection.
An independent evaluation found that 98% of participating carers reported improvements in their physical and/or mental health. These numbers represent people moving from isolation towards friendship, from financial insecurity towards opportunity, and from being overlooked towards being heard.
There are encouraging signs of wider change. Carers ID cards introduced in Dhaka last year acknowledge the contribution carers make and help them access priority services.
Salma, a recipient, said: “Within my family and society, I was without recognition. Now, my value and recognition within my family have increased.” The initiative aims to reach more than a thousand carers.
Bangladesh has a chance to lead. New social protection systems must identify unpaid family carers, not only the people receiving care, and recognize the financial costs they bear.
Health services should offer carers medical care, mental health support, and respite. Flexible livelihoods and carers’ groups should be part of community development, and carers themselves must have a voice in shaping policy.
The community volunteer network proposed in the National Healthy Ageing Strategy offers a promising starting point. It could finally provide an answer to parents who ask: “Who will care for my loved one when I am no longer here?”
This approach deserves a place in the broader National Health Policy, so that support extends beyond older people to families caring for people with disabilities and long-term conditions.
On the International Day of Care and Support, October 29, we should celebrate carers’ extraordinary contribution. But gratitude is not enough.
The real measure of progress is whether someone like Kohinoor can care for her daughter without sacrificing her own health and future. We must make that support a right, not a matter of chance.
Those who care for others deserve care too. It is time for Bangladesh to care for the carers.
Anil Patil is the Founder and Executive Director of Carers Worldwide. Anil has 25 years’ experience in the international development sector as a veterinarian, development worker, grant maker, and trustee.

item.title: A prisoner list is not protection
item.description:
The execution of two Bangladeshi citizens in Saudi Arabia's Makkah province on October 14, 2026, raises a challenging question: What is the purpose of consular protection if the government is unable to determine which of its nationals are at risk of execution until it is too late?
According to Saudi officials, two people, Nazerul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhter, have been sentenced to death after a court found them guilty of alleged immoral behavior in a mosque.
The Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah stated that it had not received advance notice of the executions. Further study found a disturbing feature. Saudi officials furnished them with a roster of nearly 2,500 offenders, including their names, but not details of their capital sentences.
Under Article 36 of the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, foreign nationals in detention have the right to communicate with and have access to consular officials.
If a detained citizen requests consular aid, the consular post shall be notified without delay, and the detainee shall be informed of this right.
Article 37(a) concerns the notification of the death of a foreign national, if the receiving authorities have the essential information. The Convention does not oblige a state to give prior notification of every execution to be carried out. Whether it violated them depends on confidential variables such as the conditions of imprisonment and whether consular notice was requested.
Bangladesh should obtain the required information rather than bring a bogus legal accusation. A bilateral system needs to be created for prompt notification of capital charges, death sentences, appeals, and scheduled executions.
The amount of Bangladesh's reliance on Saudi Arabia makes this a serious matter. In 2025, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment, and Training stated that 752,715 Bangladeshis sought employment in Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia remained the greatest provider of remittances to Bangladesh in fiscal year 2025-26, totalling more than $5.85 billion.
The enumeration named the two executed individuals but made no mention of the imposition of death sentences. The reported offenses prevented consular officials from reliably associating the entries with the executions.
It cannot guide a task that requires immediate engagement unless it specifies the allegation, the phase of processes, the verdict, the status of appeals, and the next important date.
Other nations demonstrate the operation of various components inside such a system. The Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act of the Philippines creates a Legal Assistant for Migrant Workers' Affairs and a Legal Assistance Fund to reimburse qualified expenses such as foreign attorney fees and litigation costs.
Its relevance stems from the distribution of accountability and funding for legal action, rather than relying on improvised remedies. India's MADAD consular grievance portal offers a unique feature: Citizens can lodge grievances and track their progress within the government's consular framework.
Although grievance monitoring alone cannot prevent an execution, a similar platform could enable Bangladesh to record detention conditions, assign tasks, verify timetables, and escalate lingering issues.
Indonesia provides a warning example. Siti Zainab, an Indonesian domestic servant, was executed in Saudi Arabia in 2015, despite efforts by Indonesian MPs to secure a pardon and Jakarta's concerns about the lack of prior information to her family and diplomatic authorities.
The example demonstrates that diplomatic entreaties alone cannot ensure security. Robust precautions must be taken before a problem reaches a critical stage.
For someone accused of a capital crime, time is more than just a bureaucratic issue. Timely consular intervention can help educate families, find a suitable local attorney, provide translation assistance, obtain judicial rulings, and track appeal deadlines.
It may also provide authorities with an opportunity to consider clemency or alternative sentencing, depending on the area's legislation. These opportunities are lost as the execution begins.
Bangladesh cannot assume that every conviction is invalid and cannot ask Saudi courts to abandon jurisdiction. However, it may be argued that consular protection is important and that families are not left to seek necessary answers following an irreversible ruling. Advising migrants to follow the laws of their host country is risky because it does not provide them with legal protection if arrested.
Bangladesh should demand the full judicial records of both events and provide families with verifiable information. There needs to be a proper internal evaluation of the measures to receive, evaluate, and implement the list of inmates.
Dhaka and Riyadh should set up a formal bilateral consular mechanism, whereby they would be required to inform on important criminal allegations, death sentences, appellate rulings, and scheduled executions in a timely manner.
In high-risk scenarios, Bangladesh should have an accurate, up-to-date list of the incarcerated citizens and identified authorities. Each record shall contain the name of the inmate, the charge, the judicial status, the sentence, the legal counsel, and the pertinent dates.
Create a dedicated fund for legal aid to support local lawyers, provide translation services, and hasten legal reviews. The number of detainees supported, the number of cases raised, and the outcomes should be regularly reported to the public, while respecting the confidentiality of personal information.
Bangladesh can learn from the Philippines’ financial framework and India’s case-monitoring system, but neither can be rolled out immediately. The Indonesian situation indicates that diplomatic protests after an execution don’t work. A strong system requires verifiable data from host countries, appropriate staffing and finance at foreign missions, and clear accountability in Dhaka.
In my 2020 Op-Ed for the Dhaka Tribune, "Is anyone listening?" I highlighted my concern for the safety of Bangladeshi citizens whose livelihoods rely on migration. That is the inquiry.
A prisoner roster is useless unless it motivates people to act. Bangladesh must ensure that when an individual receives a death sentence abroad, the diplomatic mission is promptly alerted so that it can investigate, acquire legal aid, and pursue all available options.
Md Fahmedul Islam Dewan is a Lecturer, Department of Law, World University of Bangladesh.

item.title: Fertiliser shortages, rising costs worry onion farmers in Faridpur
item.description:
Murikata onion farmers in Faridpur are struggling with rising production costs amid alleged shortages of fertiliser and fuel, higher labour wages and increasing prices of agricultural inputs, raising concerns over production and profitability in the new season.
Murikata onions play an important role in supplying the winter market, particularly when onion supplies from other regions remain relatively low. Farmers in Faridpur and Pabna, two key production areas, fear that rising cultivation costs and difficulties in obtaining fertiliser could affect production and push up market prices.
Farmers said they were unable to obtain adequate supplies of diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertiliser despite paying prices well above the government-fixed rate.
Although the official price of DAP fertiliser is Tk 1,050 per bag, some farmers alleged they had to pay Tk 1,600 to Tk 1,800 per bag, yet still failed to secure the quantities they needed.
The cost of onion bulbs used for planting has also increased, with farmers paying Tk 2,800 to Tk 3,000 per maund. Higher expenses for land preparation, irrigation, planting and crop maintenance, along with rising labour wages and fuel costs, have further increased their financial burden.
Rahim Molla, Abul Kalam and Jakir Sheikh, among several Murikata onion growers in the Ambikapur fields of Faridpur Sadar upazila, said rising input costs were making cultivation increasingly difficult.
They said the prices of agricultural inputs were increasing faster than the selling prices of farm produce, leaving them uncertain about earning a satisfactory return on their investments. Lower yields or a decline in onion prices could expose them to further losses, they added.
Onion growers in Char Madhabdia, including Tuhin Mondal, Azmal Bepari and Hossain Sheikh, called for an adequate supply of fertiliser at fair prices from the beginning of the season.
They also urged the authorities to ensure fuel availability and strengthen market monitoring to prevent excessive pricing of agricultural inputs.
Without fair selling prices that reflect production costs, sustaining Murikata onion cultivation could become increasingly difficult, they warned.
Anwar Hossain, agriculture officer of Faridpur Sadar upazila, said Murikata onions were important for maintaining supplies in the winter market.
Any disruption to production could affect market supply and put pressure on onion prices, he said.
Advocate Manik Majumder, president of the Faridpur Farmers’ Association, said government subsidies would have limited impact if farmers could not obtain fertiliser, pesticides and other essential agricultural inputs in the required quantities and at the right time.
He urged the relevant authorities to strengthen oversight of fertiliser distribution and market management to ensure that farmers could buy essential inputs at fair prices.
Shahadujjaman, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Faridpur, said the cultivation target for summer onions in the current Kharif-2 season had been set at 5,885 hectares.
Ensuring the supply of agricultural inputs, controlling production costs and securing fair prices for harvested produce would be important to achieving the target, he said.
The department was providing cultivation advice to farmers and encouraging them to use organic fertiliser as an alternative to chemical fertilisers, he added.
Advocate Shipra Goswami, vice-president of the Faridpur chapter of the Committee of Concerned Citizens (Shujan), said increasing agricultural production required more than expanding cultivated land.
Timely supplies of fertiliser and fuel, along with market prices that reflected production costs, were equally important, she said.
Without such measures, rising expenses could reduce farmers’ profits and threaten both Murikata onion production and the continuity of market supplies, she added.

item.title: Social alliance announces 10 demands, Dhaka-Mymensingh long march on Nov 20
item.description:
Concerns over fundamentalism, mob violence and religious and cultural persecution have prompted a social alliance to demand stronger measures to ensure justice and citizen security, alongside a series of nationwide programs, including a Dhaka-Mymensingh long march scheduled for November 20.
Sauharder Bangladesh announced 10 demands addressing these issues and outlined its planned programs to press for their implementation.
The alliance will submit memorandums through deputy commissioners in all 64 districts from November 3 to 5 and directly to the prime minister on November 5. Human chains, demonstrations, oath-taking and torch processions will be held on November 13 to press for the demands.
The demands and programs were announced at a press conference at the National Press Club on October 28. The event focused on preventing religious extremism by bringing together Sufi, Sunni, Sanatan, Buddhist, Christian, communist, Baul, Indigenous and culture-conscious people.
The alliance said it aims to establish a secular, democratic and humane Bangladesh. Its members include representatives of religious and ethnic communities, Baul-Fakir practitioners, artists, lawyers, intellectuals, judges, retired military officers, political and social organizations that uphold the spirit of the Liberation War, and other pro-democracy and secular citizens.
It said it would work peacefully and through lawful means to protect citizens' lives, freedom, beliefs, culture and dignity.
The alliance demanded impartial investigations and exemplary punishment for attacks carried out in the name of mobs against shrines, temples, akharas, khanqahs, darbars, cultural institutions such as Udichi and Chhayanaut, newspaper offices such as Prothom Alo and The Daily Star, political party offices, residential areas targeted because of residents' beliefs, and other lawful institutions and activities.
These include jatra, theatre, musical events, urs, puja, fairs, concerts and girls' sporting competitions.
It also demanded state compensation and rehabilitation for affected individuals, families, communities and institutions, along with equal security for all lawful religious, political, social and cultural institutions and practices.
The alliance demanded an immediate end to child abuse, forced sexual abuse and rape in madrasas. It called for strict measures, new legislation if necessary, and maximum punishment for those responsible for past incidents of sexual abuse in madrasas.
The alliance demanded that the state not prohibit or restrict peaceful activities such as urs, fairs, puja, religious ceremonies, girls' sporting events, cultural programs and concerts on security grounds.
It said the state must address security threats rather than shut down events and must ensure an open, safe and nondiscriminatory environment for religious, cultural and artistic activities.
The alliance called for impartial investigations and exemplary punishment for killings and violence committed because of religious beliefs or disbelief. It cited the cases of Maulana Rais Uddin, who it said was targeted for being a Sufi; Dipu Chandra Das, for being Hindu; Fakir Shamim al-Jahangir, for being a Fakir; Wahiduzzaman Shamim, over alleged religious insult; and writers and literary figures killed in the name of blogger killings.
It also demanded an impartial investigation into the killings of Ganapati Chakraborty and his family in Rangpur, with the actual perpetrators brought to justice.
The alliance called for legal action and exemplary punishment over attacks allegedly carried out in the name of religious insult, including attacks against Hindus in Dowarabazar and Tahirpur in Sunamganj, Sufis in Homna in Comilla, and a Baul practitioner in Manikganj.
It also demanded justice for violence committed in the name of protecting religion against people whose bodies were subjected to violence after death, including Nural Pagla.
The alliance said demands to declare any community non-Muslim violated citizens' rights and public security. It called for such demands to be treated as militant and anti-state activities and for legal measures to be taken.
It further demanded that the state refrain from identifying citizens by their religion and protect their personal information.
The alliance demanded the abolition of burdensome permission requirements for organizing urs, saying devotees and followers should be able to hold the events without repeatedly seeking authorization.
The alliance demanded protection for the right to carry religious and spiritual symbols, including the hair and matted locks of Baul-Fakir practitioners.
It called for strict punishment for forcibly cutting hair or matted locks, attacking or insulting religious symbols, imposing social boycotts, intimidation and psychological persecution.
It also opposed attacks, assaults and social or psychological pressure against Baul, Fakir, Sufi and Hindu ascetic communities, as well as groups that worship folk deities or spiritual powers, in the name of religious purification.
The alliance said traditional Bangladeshi folk practices must not be targeted by labeling them kufr, shirk, bidah or Hindu practices.
It also demanded protection for local folk spiritual beliefs and practices associated with trees, rivers, hills, mounds, stones and other places. Such beliefs must not be dismissed as superstition to justify destroying related objects or obstructing practices, it said, calling for lawful and environmentally appropriate preservation measures.
The alliance demanded swift and exemplary justice for violence against women, including organized attacks, harassment in the name of mobs, rape, sexual violence, insults, harassment over clothing, attacks over ornaments such as nose rings or forehead decorations, obstruction of girls' sports and cultural activities, and child marriage.
It called for adult women's freedom to make decisions about their lives, bodies, clothing, beliefs, education, professions, movement, culture and sports to be protected.
It also demanded workplace security and paid maternity leave for women workers during pregnancy.
Before women workers are sent abroad, including to the Middle East, the alliance demanded state-level security agreements with destination countries, protection of labor rights and effective complaint mechanisms. It said no woman worker should be sent abroad without these safeguards.
The alliance demanded the appointment of imams and muezzins from the Sufi community at traditional shrines across the country, including those of Shahjalal, Shah Paran, Shah Ali, Kalla Shahid, Shah Sultan Balkhi, Shah Sultan Qadruddin Rumi, Khan Jahan Ali and Bayezid Bostami.
It said people from the Qawmi, Wahhabi, Salafi and Ahl-e-Hadith traditions, as well as the Maududi school of thought, should not be appointed to these traditional Sufi institutions.
The alliance also demanded that shrine mutawallis belong to the Sufi order of the respective shrine's Sufi founder, head the shrine's board of trustees and be accountable only to the court. It called for amendments to the Waqf Act to revoke local administration's powers over shrines.
It further demanded the return of historic lakhiraj properties to shrines and khanqahs under laws issued by the Sultans and Nawabs of Bengal, arguing that those laws should take precedence over British laws in this matter.
The alliance demanded the abolition of vested or enemy property laws and the return of land to Hindu citizens living in Bangladesh or abroad in accordance with Cadastral Survey (CS) records.
It called for ownership and inheritance decisions to consider relevant historical documents, records and court rulings alongside CS records. It also demanded special measures against illegal occupation, forged deeds, administrative irregularities and land grabbing.
Release of Sanatani rights movement activists
The alliance demanded an impartial and fair review of cases involving people arrested or imprisoned for campaigning to protect the existence, security and constitutional rights of the Sanatani community, including Chinmoy Krishna Das Brahmachari.
It called for the prompt release, in accordance with the law, of those facing cases solely for peaceful and lawful expression or activism where there is no credible evidence of a crime.
